# Boundaries and drift change memory error over long delays {#ch:MEMORY-LONG-DELAYS} A rate of random spreading measured near one stored value does not yet tell us how memory error behaves after a long wait. The value may approach a boundary, wrap around an angular range, or reach a region where the spreading rate differs. A consistent movement of the average value would also change the error without being captured by the rate of random spreading alone. We begin by following the distribution of stored values across repeated trials, using the local diffusion coefficient derived in the preceding chapter. This shows why errors can keep growing on a line but level off when angular error is measured within one turn. We then separate random spreading from systematic drift and make the noise assumptions explicit. Finally, the paper's figures show what its network simulations test and distinguish movement of the memory from uncertainty when another circuit reads it. That second uncertainty motivates the information calculation that follows. Here $\theta$ is the current stored value and $\Theta$ its common initial value across trials. The local diffusion coefficient $D(\theta)$ comes from the weak spike fluctuations derived in the [preceding chapter](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-diffusion), after stable disturbances have relaxed. For constant $D$, displacement variance is $2Dt$ before boundaries matter and when there is no systematic drift. ## Long delay errors depend on boundaries and local diffusion {#sec:MEMORY-LONG-TIME} A local diffusion coefficient answers how variance initially grows. It does not by itself say that variance grows at the same rate forever. Boundaries and variation of $D$ can change the long time behavior. Let $p(\theta,t)$ be the density of the memory coordinate across repeated trials initialized at $\Theta$. The [**Itô convention**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} evaluates a state-dependent noise coefficient at the beginning of each increment. In the zero-drift diffusion approximation, this density evolves according to the [**Fokker Planck equation**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}: $$ \frac{\partial p}{\partial t} =\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}[D(\theta)p], \qquad p(\theta,0)=\delta(\theta-\Theta). $$ Here the [**Dirac delta**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} denotes a point mass: initially all probability is at $\Theta$. It differs from the earlier zero-or-one symbol $\delta_{ij}$. For constant $D$ on an unbounded line, the Gaussian solution is $$ p(\theta,t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi Dt}} \exp\left[-\frac{(\theta-\Theta)^2}{4Dt}\right]. $$ Its variance is $2Dt$. For an angular coordinate, add the densities at all displacements $\theta-\Theta+2\pi k$, $k\in\mathbb Z$, to wrap the Gaussian around the circle. This wrapped sum appears in [SI Eq. S31, p. 7](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=7&zoom=125,0,483). At long times the density approaches $1/(2\pi)$. If angular errors are reported in $[-\pi,\pi)$, their limiting mean squared value is $$ \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}x^2dx=\frac{\pi^2}{3}. $$ The flattening of a ring network's error curve can therefore occur while its local noise mechanism remains unchanged. It reflects the bounded way angular error is reported.[^p1-fp] For $D=0.5\,\mathrm{rad}^2/\mathrm{s}$, the plots show how the density and squared error change with delay.
{{block:fig:MEMORY-LINE-RING}}
As the upper density approaches uniform, the wrapped error below approaches $\pi^2/3$; the line error keeps growing. ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Derivation: from random increments to the memory density equation"} To pass from random increments to a density equation, choose any smooth function $F(\theta)$. In a short interval $dt$, the zero-drift Itô increment has conditional mean zero and conditional second moment $2D(\theta)dt$. Taylor expansion at the starting coordinate gives $$ \begin{aligned} \mathbb E[F(\theta+d\theta)-F(\theta)\mid\theta] &=F'(\theta)\mathbb E[d\theta\mid\theta] +\tfrac12F''(\theta)\mathbb E[(d\theta)^2\mid\theta]+o(dt)\\ &=D(\theta)F''(\theta)dt+o(dt). \end{aligned} $$ The higher-order terms vanish faster than $dt$ in this diffusion approximation. Averaging over the starting-coordinate density and dividing by $dt$ gives $$ \frac{d}{dt}\int F(\theta)p(\theta,t)\,d\theta =\int F''(\theta)D(\theta)p(\theta,t)\,d\theta. $$ Take $F$ to vanish outside an interior region, or use boundaries for which the integration terms vanish. Integrating by parts twice moves both derivatives from $F$ onto the product $Dp$. Because the resulting identity holds for every such smooth $F$, it gives the Fokker Planck equation shown above. ::: When $D$ varies with state, the zero drift stochastic equation is $d\theta=\sqrt{2D(\theta)}\,dB$ with the Itô convention. Under conditions that remove boundary terms, the density equation gives $$ \frac{d}{dt}E[\theta]=0, \qquad \frac{d}{dt}\operatorname{Var}(\theta)=2E[D(\theta)]. $$ To obtain these identities, multiply the density equation by $\theta$ or $(\theta-\Theta)^2$, integrate over $\theta$, and integrate by parts twice. The second derivatives of these functions are respectively zero and two, giving the two identities. A similar calculation for the smooth function $D$ gives $dE[D]/dt=E[DD'']$. Expanding at $t=0$ therefore yields $$ \operatorname{Var}(\theta) =2D(\Theta)t+D(\Theta)D''(\Theta)t^2+O(t^3). $$ This is [SI Eq. S37, p. 8](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=8&zoom=125,0,602). A state dependent $D$ need not produce a curved variance versus time graph. If $D$ is linear in $\theta$, then $E[D(\theta)]=D(E[\theta])=D(\Theta)$, so the variance remains linear while the process stays within the model's valid domain.[^p1-variable] The supplement illustrates this with mutual excitation, $W_{12}=W_{21}=1$, biases $(b_0,-b_0)$, and the same linear transfer rule. The fixed activation states are $(\theta+b_0/2,\theta-b_0/2)$. Now $\mathbf u=(1,1)^T$, $\mathbf v=(1/2,1/2)^T$, and $$ 2D=\frac{1}{4}(\bar r_1+\bar r_2)=\frac{\theta}{2\tau}, \qquad D=\frac{\theta}{4\tau}. $$ The implied variance is $\Theta t/(2\tau)$, agreeing with [SI Eq. S41, p. 9](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=9&zoom=125,0,383) and the slope tested in [Fig. S1, p. 10](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=10&zoom=125,0,45). SI Eq. S40 instead prints $D=\theta/(2\tau)$. Under the convention used throughout this guide, that displayed value differs by a factor of two from the direct projection and S41.[^p1-excitation] ## A diffusion calculation does not determine systematic drift {#sec:MEMORY-DRIFT-SCOPE} Repeated trials can spread apart even if their average stays at the original value. That random spreading differs from a reproducible movement in one direction. Both can occur, and the derivation of $D$ alone does not settle the second question. The paper assumes that the network is tuned to eliminate [**systematic drift**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, meaning a nonzero mean velocity along the attractor. A deterministic mismatch in weights can create such a velocity. In addition, state dependent noise and curved network dynamics can create a small mean motion even if the noise free model has an exact continuous attractor. The supplement explains that deriving the exact mean motion requires the microscopic jump process, beyond the leading variance calculation ([SI “Systematic drift,” pp. 4–5](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=4&zoom=125,0,362)).[^p1-systematic] For state dependent $D$, where the coefficient is evaluated affects the process. The [**Stratonovich convention**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} uses midpoint evaluation in its limiting increments. With the same written coefficient and zero written drift, it describes a different process from the Itô equation. Converting the Stratonovich equation into Itô form adds a drift $D'/2$. This follows from the conversion term $bb'/2$ with $b=\sqrt{2D}$ and $bb'=D'$. The supplement uses the difference to estimate a possible scale of noise induced drift, not to identify the exact drift of every neural network. With $D$ of order $1/N$, random displacement over $dt$ is of order $\sqrt{dt/N}$, while such a mean displacement is of order $dt/N$. The variance calculation captures the leading random term. Small changes to weights or biases might cancel the mean drift; they cannot remove the random increments by subtracting a known average. A known mean drift can in principle be accounted for by a decoder, but any actual implementation must know that drift and respect the domain and boundary conditions. The independence assumption also has a precise scope. Newly generated spike-count fluctuations are conditionally independent given the present state. Shared recurrent fluctuations can still correlate the observed spike trains over time. An extra source of correlated fluctuations would change the projection formula to $2D=\mathbf v^TQ\mathbf v$, where $Q\,dt$ is their increment covariance. Calculating the corresponding Fisher information would require the matching joint likelihood. The paper discusses such correlated models as future extensions ([Discussion, p. 5, paragraph beginning “Our spiking model”](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf#page=5&zoom=125,0,142)); it does not prove that every correlated spiking model obeys its Poisson formulas.[^p1-correlation] ## Figures distinguish memory motion from readout error and test diffusion {#sec:MEMORY-FIGURES} [Figure 1A, p. 2](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf#page=2&zoom=125,0,439) shows the definition of the memory coordinate. Start at a green point off the attractor and follow the noise free flow to the black point on it. This endpoint defines the instantaneous attractor state. After one noisy interval, repeat that flow. The difference between the two endpoints is the retained memory change. The relevant projection follows the flow, as in the [tilted two variable example](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-linearization). In Fig. 1B, an [**activity bump**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a localized peak of population firing rates across the neurons' preferred angles. The figure separates two sources of error: - During storage, the bump's location has moved away from its initial value $\Theta$. - At the later time, an observer has additional uncertainty about the bump's current location because it sees only a finite sample of spikes. The [information calculation](ch-memory-information.html#sec-memory-fi) measures this second uncertainty and relates it to diffusion; the [readout chapter](ch-memory-readout.html) then follows observation of the moving state.[^p1-fig1] [Figure 2, p. 3](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf#page=3&zoom=125,0,18) tests the diffusion calculation in two different network designs. Panel A shows a ring with weights determined by differences of preferred angles. This gives rotational symmetry: rotating the activity pattern around the ring leaves its dynamics unchanged in form. In B, compare the firing rate curves and spike marks in the inset before reading the wandering angular trace. The curve describes rates; the marks are particular random spike events. The trace shows the represented angle rather than overall activity amplitude. Panels C and D test different parts of the prediction: - Panel C compares simulated mean squared angular displacements with the prediction from the tuning curves and transfer function. The gray exponential case and black sigmoidal, or S-shaped, case have different transfer functions. The dashed bound is a lower limit for the sigmoidal case, not a separate fitted trajectory. A model can lie above its information bound while still agreeing with the derived diffusion formula. - Panel D follows angular error to longer intervals; its flattening uses angular wrapping, not a disappearance of noise. The expected limiting value with the caption's error convention is $\pi^2/3$. Panels E to G use mutual inhibition rather than a ring. The two rates in F vary in opposite directions; their difference represents memory. Panel G compares their displacement statistics with the analytic prediction. This second design matters because the projection argument does not require rotational symmetry. These are simulations checking the model calculation. They are not direct measurements of memory noise in an animal.[^p1-fig2] The derivation has now supplied a dynamical quantity, $D$, from spike variability and the way a network returns to its attractor. # Spike information limits memory stability {#ch:MEMORY-INFORMATION} A neuron that receives spikes from a memory circuit can use them to estimate the value stored by that circuit. Burak and Fiete connect these two effects by deriving a lower bound on memory diffusion from the information in the spikes.[^p1-info-main] The useful quantity is how clearly a short spike sample distinguishes nearby memory values. This is a limit for a particular network, so using it to compare different networks also requires keeping track of what changes and what stays fixed. We retain the memory coordinate $\theta$, initial value $\Theta$, firing rate $\bar r_i(\theta)$, synaptic time constant $\tau$, and diffusion convention $\operatorname{Var}(\Delta\theta)=2D\Delta t$. The [network projection](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-linearization) determines which activity changes remain as changes in the stored value. ## Rate slopes and spike variability determine local information {#sec:MEMORY-FI} Suppose two nearby memory values produce almost identical rates. A short spike sample cannot reliably tell them apart. If a small change in memory instead produces a large rate change relative to spike variability, that sample is more useful. We need a quantity that measures this local distinction. A [**likelihood**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the probability of observed data as a function of a proposed parameter value. In a short interval $h$, let $n_i$ be neuron $i$'s count. Treat the state as locally constant and use the conditional independent Poisson approximation. Then $$ p(\mathbf n\mid\theta)=\prod_i \frac{[\bar r_i(\theta)h]^{n_i}e^{-\bar r_i(\theta)h}}{n_i!}. $$ Taking the logarithm turns the product into a sum. With $r_i'=d\bar r_i/d\theta$, $$ \ell(\theta)=\log p(\mathbf n\mid\theta) =\sum_i\{n_i\log[\bar r_i(\theta)h]-\bar r_i(\theta)h-\log(n_i!)\}, $$ $$ S(\theta)=\frac{d\ell}{d\theta} =\sum_i\frac{r_i'}{\bar r_i}(n_i-\bar r_i h). $$ The [**score**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} $S$ measures how the log likelihood changes when the proposed memory value changes. Its mean is zero because $E[n_i]=\bar r_i h$. Its mean square is $$ E[S^2] =\sum_i\frac{(r_i')^2}{\bar r_i^2}\operatorname{Var}(n_i) =h\sum_i\frac{(r_i')^2}{\bar r_i}. $$ The cross terms vanish by conditional independence, and Poisson variance supplies $\operatorname{Var}(n_i)=\bar r_i h$. [**Fisher information**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is this expected squared score. The paper divides it by observation duration and calls the result the [**internal Fisher information rate**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}: $$ \boxed{J(\theta)=\sum_i\frac{(r_i')^2}{\bar r_i}.} $$ If the coordinate is an angle in radians, $J$ has units $\mathrm{rad}^{-2}\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The information in a locally stationary interval of duration $h$ is $Jh$, not $J$. We write formulas for positive rates; a vanishing rate requires a suitable limit and regularity of the likelihood.[^p1-fi-source] Each cell contributes squared slope divided by its count variance per unit time. High rates with zero slope do not distinguish neighboring values, so they contribute no local information. A sharply changing rate can be informative even if it is smaller than another cell's peak rate. The coordinate here describes the network's present internal state. It need not be a currently visible external stimulus. Sensory Fisher information has the same Poisson formula only when the stimulus dependent tuning curves are the relevant rates. Two positive tuning curves with the same changing part isolate the effect of extra baseline firing.

The rate peak has zero local slope, so it contributes no local information at that point. Extra spikes from a constant baseline increase Poisson variability without making nearby values easier to distinguish. See [Internal Fisher information, Eq. 3, p. 2](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf#page=2). To understand why inverse information is an error scale, let $\hat\theta(\mathbf n)$ be an estimator whose mean equals $\theta$ locally. Such an estimator is [**unbiased**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. Differentiate $E_\theta[\hat\theta]=\theta$ with respect to $\theta$. Under the usual conditions allowing differentiation through the sum over data, $$ 1=\sum_{\mathbf n}\hat\theta(\mathbf n)\partial_\theta p(\mathbf n\mid\theta) =E[\hat\theta S] =E[(\hat\theta-\theta)S]. $$ The last equality uses $E[S]=0$. Cauchy Schwarz now gives $$ 1\le E[(\hat\theta-\theta)^2]E[S^2], \qquad \boxed{\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta)\ge\frac{1}{Jh}.} $$ This is the [**Cramér Rao bound**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. It is a local bound for regular unbiased estimation. It does not guarantee that every finite spike sample admits an estimator attaining it. The paper works in a weak noise, informative sample regime where local likelihoods can be approximated as Gaussian and efficient estimation can approach the bound. A [**prior distribution**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} represents knowledge about likely parameter values before observing the spikes. A strong prior, bias, boundaries, or globally ambiguous tuning changes the estimation problem.[^p1-cr] ## Spike information sets a lower bound on memory diffusion {#sec:MEMORY-BOUND} The network has no access to its exact firing rates as noiseless numbers. Its recurrent input is built from the same random spikes that an external observer sees. The lower bound on diffusion follows directly by comparing the state sensitivity of the network with the spike information. From the [projection and diffusion calculation](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-diffusion), $$ 2D=\sum_i v_i^2\bar r_i, \qquad u_i=\tau r_i', \qquad \sum_i v_i u_i=1. $$ Define two vectors $a_i=v_i\sqrt{\bar r_i}$ and $b_i=r_i'/\sqrt{\bar r_i}$. Their dot product is $$ \sum_i a_i b_i=\sum_i v_i r_i'=\frac{1}{\tau}. $$ Their squared lengths are $\sum_i a_i^2=2D$ and $\sum_i b_i^2=J$. Cauchy Schwarz therefore gives $$ \left(\frac1\tau\right)^2 \le\left(\sum_i a_i^2\right)\left(\sum_i b_i^2\right)=2DJ, $$ or $$ \boxed{D\ge\frac{1}{2\tau^2J}.} $$ This proof uses the general left vector formula, so symmetric weights are unnecessary. It is a shorter teaching reconstruction of the scalar proof in SI Section V. Its assumptions are those used to derive $D$ and $J$; it is not a general statement about all possible noisy memory systems.[^p1-bound-source] The units agree: $\tau^2J$ has units of time per coordinate squared, so its reciprocal has the units of diffusion. Small internal information forces a large minimum diffusion coefficient. Large information allows small diffusion, but does not guarantee it. Equality requires the two vectors in the proof to be proportional: $$ v_i=c\frac{r_i'}{\bar r_i} \quad\text{for every contributing cell}, \qquad c=\frac{1}{\tau J}. $$ Cells with zero tuning slope cannot contribute extra projected noise if equality is to hold. In a symmetric network, $v_i$ is proportional to $g_i'$, and $r_i'=\phi'(\bar g_i)g_i'$. At each state, the participating cells therefore need a common value of $\phi'(\bar g_i)/\phi(\bar g_i)$. A sufficient way to satisfy this at all states is to choose that ratio equal to the same constant $k$ throughout the relevant input range. Solving $$ \frac{d}{dg}\log\phi(g)=k $$ gives $\phi(g)=A e^{kg}$. This exponential family attains equality for symmetric weights with Poisson noise, under the other model assumptions. It is a sufficient condition, rather than a general necessity: the common ratio may depend on the current memory state.[^p1-equality] ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Check: equality can also hold with a linear transfer rule"} The [mutual-excitation example](ch-memory-long-delays.html#sec-memory-long-time) supplies a counterexample to the unrestricted converse. Set its bias $b_0=0$ and use the linear rule $\phi(g)=g/\tau$ on positive inputs. Its fixed states are $s_1=s_2=\theta>0$, with $\mathbf u=(1,1)^T$ and $\mathbf v=(1/2,1/2)^T$. Both rates are $\theta/\tau$, and both rate derivatives are $1/\tau$. Therefore $$ 2D=\frac{\theta}{2\tau},\qquad J=\frac{2}{\tau\theta},\qquad 2DJ=\frac{1}{\tau^2}. $$ Equality holds throughout this family even though its transfer rule is linear. At each state both cells receive the same input, and the ratio $\phi'/\phi=1/\theta$ changes between states. A converse that forces an exponential rule needs additional restrictions linking the participating input values across cells and states. Continuous variation of the represented value alone does not supply them. This qualification concerns the source's claimed converse, while leaving the information–diffusion inequality intact. ::: **Example: the same diffusion with a looser information bound.** In the two cell mutual inhibition model, use $b=200$ activation units and $\tau=0.1\,\mathrm{s}$. The memory coordinate is an activation difference, not an angle. At $\theta=0$ both rates are $1000\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ and their slopes are $\pm5\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ per activation unit. Thus $$ J=\frac{25}{1000}+\frac{25}{1000}=0.05, \qquad D=\frac{b}{2\tau}=1000. $$ Here $J$ has units of inverse activation unit squared per second, and $D$ has activation unit squared per second. The bound is $1/(2\tau^2J)=1000$, so equality holds at this balanced state. At $\theta=100$, the rates become $1500$ and $500\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, while their slopes stay $\pm5$. Now $$ J=\frac{25}{1500}+\frac{25}{500}=\frac1{15}\simeq0.06667, \qquad \frac1{2\tau^2J}=750. $$ The actual diffusion remains $1000$. The inequality is strict because these two unequal rates no longer align the network's projection weights with the information optimal weights. This also shows why equality at a special state does not force the transfer function to be exponential on its whole domain. A constant lower bound attained everywhere and an accidental equality at one state are different claims.
{{block:fig:MEMORY-BOUND-STRICTNESS}}
The gap at $\theta=100$ shows why a lower minimum allowed by the inequality is not a reduction in the network’s actual diffusion. See [Diffusion bound, Eq. 4, p. 3](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf#page=3). For $m$ memory coordinates the information is a matrix, $$ J_{\alpha\beta}=\sum_i \frac{\partial_{\theta_\alpha}\bar r_i\, \partial_{\theta_\beta}\bar r_i}{\bar r_i}. $$ The matrix bound $2D\succeq\tau^{-2}J^{-1}$ means that every linear combination of coordinate displacements obeys the corresponding variance lower bound. Here $A\succeq B$ means $\mathbf z^T(A-B)\mathbf z\ge0$ for every real vector $\mathbf z$. To derive it, form $N\times m$ matrices $U_{i\alpha}=u_i^\alpha/\sqrt{\bar r_i}$ and $V_{i\alpha}=v_i^\alpha\sqrt{\bar r_i}$. Then $$ U^TV=I,\qquad U^TU=\tau^2J,\qquad V^TV=2D. $$ The matrix inequality applies when every independent small coordinate change can be distinguished through a change in rates, so $J$ is invertible. It also explains why a scalar bound in each coordinate separately would miss coupled directions.[^p1-matrix] ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Check: the residual matrix proves the lower bound"} Set $Q=V-U(U^TU)^{-1}$. Expanding $Q^TQ$ and using $U^TV=I$ gives $$ Q^TQ=V^TV-(U^TU)^{-1} =2D-\tau^{-2}J^{-1}\succeq0. $$ ::: ## Improving persistence depends on what a comparison holds fixed {#sec:MEMORY-COMPARISONS} The inequality compares diffusion and information for the same network. To compare different networks, we must say what stays fixed. Otherwise an apparent benefit of a parameter change may come from changing another property at the same time. Increasing $N$ while retaining the same distribution of tuning curves and scaling weights as $1/N$ keeps individual inputs and rates fixed. The sums in the symmetric formula scale as $N$ in the numerator and $N^2$ in the denominator. Consequently $D\propto1/N$, while $J\propto N$. This is a controlled density or population replication comparison, not a promise about adding arbitrary neurons. If all tuning rates are multiplied by a factor $a$, their slopes are also multiplied by $a$, so $J\mapsto aJ$. For equality achieving exponential networks, $D\mapsto D/a$ immediately follows. The same scaling follows from the symmetric diffusion formula when the change preserves $g_i'$ up to a common scale and preserves the tuning geometry. For a general fixed nonlinear transfer rule, multiplying rates need not preserve those quantities or even the attractor. The paper's rate comparison is made with the tuning shapes and appropriate network scaling held under control.[^p1-scaling] Changing $\tau$ while holding the rate tuning curves and their input relation fixed gives $D\propto\tau^{-2}$ in the symmetric formula. Maintaining those curves requires retuning the network, because $\bar s=\tau\bar r$. In contrast, holding activation curves and dimensionless weights fixed in the linear two cell example makes rates scale as $1/\tau$, so $D=b/(2\tau)\propto\tau^{-1}$. These two statements concern different controlled comparisons. A larger cellular time constant can improve memory stability while the exponent of its effect depends on what the experiment keeps fixed. The paper also links tuning width to memory persistence. The reason for its opposite predictions in one and three dimensions can be derived from the number of active cells and their slopes. This derivation is a teaching reconstruction of the tuning width argument cited in the main text, rather than a proof that every tuning family follows one power law.[^p1-width] Assume preferred positions $\mathbf c$ have uniform density $\rho$ in a $d$ dimensional stimulus or memory space. Away from boundaries, let identical tuning curves have fixed peak rate $a$ and a common shape $f$: $$ \bar r_{\mathbf c}(\boldsymbol\theta) =a f[(\boldsymbol\theta-\mathbf c)/w]. $$ The width $w$ is varied while $a$, $\rho$, and the shape $f$ are fixed. For one coordinate direction $\alpha$, replace the population sum by an integral and substitute $\mathbf z=(\boldsymbol\theta-\mathbf c)/w$: $$ J_{\alpha\alpha} \simeq\rho\int d^d c\, \frac{a^2w^{-2}(\partial_\alpha f)^2}{af} =\rho a w^{d-2} \int d^d z\,\frac{(\partial_\alpha f)^2}{f}. $$ Two factors determine how information changes with tuning width: - The volume element contributes $w^d$ because broader fields recruit more neurons. - The squared slope contributes $w^{-2}$ because broader curves change more slowly. Each diagonal entry therefore scales as $J_{\alpha\alpha}\propto w^{d-2}$. Now restrict the tuning shape $f$ to depend only on distance from its center. Uniformly distributing those centers makes every coordinate direction equivalent: off-diagonal information terms vanish, and all diagonal entries are equal. For an exponential network that attains the matrix bound, $D_{\alpha\alpha}=1/(2\tau^2J_{\alpha\alpha})\propto w^{2-d}$. The resulting comparisons are: - Narrower curves help in $d=1$. - Width has no leading effect in $d=2$. - Broader curves help in $d=3$. These conclusions change under another resource constraint. Fixing the total population spike rate instead of peak rate makes $a\propto w^{-d}$, giving $J\propto w^{-2}$ in every dimension. Sparse coverage, a large baseline rate, finite boundaries, correlated noise, or a width too small for the population integral can also change the comparison. Attaining equality means the network reaches the diffusion lower bound for its information rate and synaptic time constant. Minimizing diffusion still requires deciding how much information the allowed architecture and firing budget can supply. If an external stimulus produces the same tuning curves as the network's input free memory states, the sensory and internal Fisher information are equal. In a symmetric exponential network, maximizing this information then improves sensory estimation and minimizes memory diffusion together. This is why the paper suggests that one circuit could support both sensory estimation and memory storage. Small internal information forces a large minimum diffusion coefficient. Large information allows small diffusion, but does not guarantee it. **Neural mechanism.** Reaching the bound requires the network's retained response to each cell's spike noise to match that cell's information about memory. A cell that adds retained noise without helping distinguish nearby values prevents equality. **Mathematical derivation.** Equality requires the two vectors in the proof to be proportional: $$ v_i=c\frac{r_i'}{\bar r_i} \quad\text{for every contributing cell}, \qquad c=\frac{1}{\tau J}. $$ Cells with zero tuning slope cannot contribute extra projected noise if equality is to hold. In a symmetric network, $v_i$ is proportional to $g_i'$, and $r_i'=\phi'(\bar g_i)g_i'$. At each state, the participating cells therefore need a common value of $\phi'(\bar g_i)/\phi(\bar g_i)$. A sufficient way to satisfy this at all states is to choose that ratio equal to the same constant $k$ throughout the relevant input range. Solving $$ \frac{d}{dg}\log\phi(g)=k $$ gives $\phi(g)=A e^{kg}$. **Interpretation.** This exponential family attains equality for symmetric weights with Poisson noise, under the other model assumptions. It is a sufficient condition, rather than a general necessity: the common ratio may depend on the current memory state.[^p1-equality] ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Check: equality can also hold with a linear transfer rule"} The [mutual-excitation example](ch-memory-long-delays.html#sec-memory-long-time) supplies a counterexample to the unrestricted converse. Set its bias $b_0=0$ and use the linear rule $\phi(g)=g/\tau$ on positive inputs. Its fixed states are $s_1=s_2=\theta>0$, with $\mathbf u=(1,1)^T$ and $\mathbf v=(1/2,1/2)^T$. Both rates are $\theta/\tau$, and both rate derivatives are $1/\tau$. Therefore $$ 2D=\frac{\theta}{2\tau},\qquad J=\frac{2}{\tau\theta},\qquad 2DJ=\frac{1}{\tau^2}. $$ Equality holds throughout this family even though its transfer rule is linear. At each state both cells receive the same input, and the ratio $\phi'/\phi=1/\theta$ changes between states. A converse that forces an exponential rule needs additional restrictions linking the participating input values across cells and states. Continuous variation of the represented value alone does not supply them. This qualification concerns the source's claimed converse, while leaving the information–diffusion inequality intact. ::: **Example: the same diffusion with a looser information bound.** In the two cell mutual inhibition model, use $b=200$ activation units and $\tau=0.1\,\mathrm{s}$. The memory coordinate is an activation difference, not an angle. At $\theta=0$ both rates are $1000\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ and their slopes are $\pm5\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ per activation unit. Thus $$ J=\frac{25}{1000}+\frac{25}{1000}=0.05, \qquad D=\frac{b}{2\tau}=1000. $$ Here $J$ has units of inverse activation unit squared per second, and $D$ has activation unit squared per second. The bound is $1/(2\tau^2J)=1000$, so equality holds at this balanced state. At $\theta=100$, the rates become $1500$ and $500\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, while their slopes stay $\pm5$. Now $$ J=\frac{25}{1500}+\frac{25}{500}=\frac1{15}\simeq0.06667, \qquad \frac1{2\tau^2J}=750. $$ The actual diffusion remains $1000$. The inequality is strict because these two unequal rates no longer align the network's projection weights with the information optimal weights. This also shows why equality at a special state does not force the transfer function to be exponential on its whole domain. A constant lower bound attained everywhere and an accidental equality at one state are different claims.
{{block:fig:MEMORY-BOUND-STRICTNESS}}
The gap at $\theta=100$ shows why a lower minimum allowed by the inequality is not a reduction in the network’s actual diffusion. See [Diffusion bound, Eq. 4, p. 3](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf#page=3). **Neural mechanism.** When a circuit stores several coordinates, a spike can shift more than one of them. Comparing each coordinate separately would miss combinations of shifts. The information and diffusion must therefore describe these shared directions. **Mathematical derivation.** For $m$ memory coordinates the information is a matrix, $$ J_{\alpha\beta}=\sum_i \frac{\partial_{\theta_\alpha}\bar r_i\, \partial_{\theta_\beta}\bar r_i}{\bar r_i}. $$ The matrix calculation assumes that every independent small coordinate change can be distinguished through a change in rates, so $J$ is invertible. The matrix bound $2D\succeq\tau^{-2}J^{-1}$ means that every linear combination of coordinate displacements obeys the corresponding variance lower bound. Here $A\succeq B$ means $\mathbf z^T(A-B)\mathbf z\ge0$ for every real vector $\mathbf z$. To derive it, form $N\times m$ matrices $U_{i\alpha}=u_i^\alpha/\sqrt{\bar r_i}$ and $V_{i\alpha}=v_i^\alpha\sqrt{\bar r_i}$. Then $$ U^TV=I,\qquad U^TU=\tau^2J,\qquad V^TV=2D. $$ ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Check: the residual matrix proves the lower bound"} Set $Q=V-U(U^TU)^{-1}$. Expanding $Q^TQ$ and using $U^TV=I$ gives $$ Q^TQ=V^TV-(U^TU)^{-1} =2D-\tau^{-2}J^{-1}\succeq0. $$ ::: **Interpretation.** The bound controls every combination of stored coordinates, including coupled directions that separate scalar bounds would miss. It applies under the rate-distinguishability condition used above; if $J$ is singular, this ordinary inverse formula cannot be used.[^p1-matrix] ## Improving persistence depends on what a comparison holds fixed {#sec:MEMORY-COMPARISONS} **Neural mechanism.** The inequality compares diffusion and information for the same network. To compare different networks, we must say what stays fixed. Otherwise an apparent benefit of a parameter change may come from changing another property at the same time. The comparisons below control how added neurons, altered firing rates, or slower synaptic decay affect the tuning curves and recurrent input. **Mathematical derivation.** Increasing $N$ while retaining the same distribution of tuning curves and scaling weights as $1/N$ keeps individual inputs and rates fixed. The sums in the symmetric formula scale as $N$ in the numerator and $N^2$ in the denominator. Consequently $D\propto1/N$, while $J\propto N$. This is a controlled density or population replication comparison, not a promise about adding arbitrary neurons. If all tuning rates are multiplied by a factor $a$, their slopes are also multiplied by $a$, so $J\mapsto aJ$. For equality achieving exponential networks, $D\mapsto D/a$ immediately follows. The same scaling follows from the symmetric diffusion formula when the change preserves $g_i'$ up to a common scale and preserves the tuning geometry. For a general fixed nonlinear transfer rule, multiplying rates need not preserve those quantities or even the attractor. The paper's rate comparison is made with the tuning shapes and appropriate network scaling held under control.[^p1-scaling] Changing $\tau$ while holding the rate tuning curves and their input relation fixed gives $D\propto\tau^{-2}$ in the symmetric formula. Maintaining those curves requires retuning the network, because $\bar s=\tau\bar r$. In contrast, holding activation curves and dimensionless weights fixed in the linear two cell example makes rates scale as $1/\tau$, so $D=b/(2\tau)\propto\tau^{-1}$. **Interpretation.** These two statements concern different controlled comparisons. A larger cellular time constant can improve memory stability while the exponent of its effect depends on what the experiment keeps fixed. **Neural mechanism.** The paper also links tuning width to memory persistence. The reason for its opposite predictions in one and three dimensions can be derived from the number of active cells and their slopes. This derivation is a teaching reconstruction of the tuning width argument cited in the main text, rather than a proof that every tuning family follows one power law.[^p1-width] Assume preferred positions $\mathbf c$ have uniform density $\rho$ in a $d$ dimensional stimulus or memory space. Away from boundaries, let identical tuning curves have fixed peak rate $a$ and a common shape $f$: $$ \bar r_{\mathbf c}(\boldsymbol\theta) =a f[(\boldsymbol\theta-\mathbf c)/w]. $$ The width $w$ is varied while $a$, $\rho$, and the shape $f$ are fixed. **Mathematical derivation.** For one coordinate direction $\alpha$, replace the population sum by an integral and substitute $\mathbf z=(\boldsymbol\theta-\mathbf c)/w$: $$ J_{\alpha\alpha} \simeq\rho\int d^d c\, \frac{a^2w^{-2}(\partial_\alpha f)^2}{af} =\rho a w^{d-2} \int d^d z\,\frac{(\partial_\alpha f)^2}{f}. $$ Two factors determine how information changes with tuning width: - The volume element contributes $w^d$ because broader fields recruit more neurons. - The squared slope contributes $w^{-2}$ because broader curves change more slowly. Each diagonal entry therefore scales as $J_{\alpha\alpha}\propto w^{d-2}$. Now restrict the tuning shape $f$ to depend only on distance from its center. Uniformly distributing those centers makes every coordinate direction equivalent: off-diagonal information terms vanish, and all diagonal entries are equal. For an exponential network that attains the matrix bound, $D_{\alpha\alpha}=1/(2\tau^2J_{\alpha\alpha})\propto w^{2-d}$. **Interpretation.** The resulting comparisons are: - Narrower curves help in $d=1$. - Width has no leading effect in $d=2$. - Broader curves help in $d=3$. These conclusions change under another resource constraint. Fixing the total population spike rate instead of peak rate makes $a\propto w^{-d}$, giving $J\propto w^{-2}$ in every dimension. Sparse coverage, a large baseline rate, finite boundaries, correlated noise, or a width too small for the population integral can also change the comparison. Attaining equality means the network reaches the diffusion lower bound for its information rate and synaptic time constant. Minimizing diffusion still requires deciding how much information the allowed architecture and firing budget can supply. If an external stimulus produces the same tuning curves as the network's input free memory states, the sensory and internal Fisher information are equal. In a symmetric exponential network, maximizing this information then improves sensory estimation and minimizes memory diffusion together. This is why the paper suggests that one circuit could support both sensory estimation and memory storage.
